pages.purpose:
A good manager understands the importance of building a strong team, not simply managing individuals. We would like to see how you approach team building and whether you can design an activity that creates genuine connection rather than simply giving people something social to do.

This scenario is taken from a real task that we had undertaken ourselves. If you were working with us, you may have been assigned this task as part of your role. We are interested in seeing how you think about the problem, what you propose, and, most importantly, the reasoning behind your decisions.

questions.scenario:
A well-established company that had been operating for more than 10 years. If you asked employees to rate their satisfaction from 1 to 10, you would consistently receive 9s and 10s.

A common comment was, "This is by far the best company I've ever worked for."

Another employee described the company as, "It's a place that makes colleges feel like family and office feel like home."

These were not hypothetical comments. They were made, and the culture described above was real.

One of the team-building traditions was a shoutout system.

Throughout the week, employees could write shoutouts for other people in the company. Recognising something they had done, thanking them for their help, or simply acknowledging something they appreciated about them.

There were around 30 full-time employees, working together in an open office.

On Friday, all of the shoutouts were printed onto pieces of paper. Each person received one. Everyone then gathered around the dining table on Friday evening. They would stand around the table and take turns reading their shoutouts aloud.

What made it powerful was not simply the fact that people were giving each other compliments.

The gathering became a symbol, like children around a campfire. Not employees following a process, but children listening to stories.
questions.questionText:
Your Task
Using this as inspiration, design a team-building activity for our company.

We are a remote startup with six employees, so your activity should be designed specifically around the realities of our team.

We want your best answer, so take your time thinking about it.

Do not focus only on what the activity is. We are particularly interested in why you have designed it the way you have.

For example:
• Why will people want to participate?
• What behaviour or feeling is the activity intended to create?
• How will it help six people who work remotely feel more connected?
• What makes the activity meaningful rather than simply "fun"?
• What rituals or recurring elements would you introduce?
• Is there an equivalent to everyone physically gathering around the dining table?
• How would you make sure everyone participates rather than allowing the more outgoing people to dominate?
• How would you make the activity feel authentic rather than like a forced corporate team-building exercise?
• How would you make it something people eventually look forward to?
• What small details would make the experience memorable?

We are less interested in an impressive-sounding activity than in seeing whether you understand the psychology and reasoning behind good team building.

The best answers will recognise that strong teams are not created simply by putting people into a Zoom call and asking them to play a game. They are created through repeated experiences that give people a sense of belonging, recognition, shared history and connection.

Think carefully about the difference between an activity people participate in and a ritual that becomes part of the identity of a team.

Final Thought
When thinking about your answer, consider what was really happening when those 30 employees stood around the dining table on a Friday evening.

Good team building is not really about games, activities or even entertainment. It is about creating those small rituals through which a group of individuals slowly becomes a tribe — a group with shared stories, shared memories and a feeling that they belong to one another.

Design something that can create that feeling for our team.
questions.placeholder: Design your team-building activity and explain your reasoning...
questions.tips: Focus on the psychology and reasoning behind your design, not just describing the activity itself.

pages.purpose:
This series of questions is designed for managerial positions. We'll place you in a realistic workplace situation and evaluate your decision-making ability.

The objective: Can you make the right decisions when there isn't a policy telling you what it is?

questions.scenario:
An intern candidate (C) joins us on Slack for a three-day trial period. On their first day, a meeting is scheduled for 6:00 PM IST to help them get started.

Around 1pm, C joins Slack and introduces themselves. At 6pm, C does not attend the meeting and does not respond to any Slack messages. At 7:00 PM IST, C's manager (M) decides to remove C from Slack and end the trial.

M's manager (SM) later gives M the following constructive feedback:

"It was C's first day, so you should have given them a second chance. At the very least, you should have waited for them to explain why they missed the meeting before deciding to fail them. What if they had a genuine emergency?"
questions.questionText: Question: If you were the manager of both M and SM, how would you handle this situation? Whose position do you agree with, and why? Do you believe M made the correct decision, or was SM right to challenge it? Explain what you believe should have been done and how you would manage both M and SM following the situation.

supportingTabs.label: Assumption
supportingTabs.content: Company policy gives managers discretion to make decisions based on their own judgement and the circumstances of each situation. There is no specific policy governing this scenario. This assumption is included so that your answer focuses on what you believe the right managerial decision is, rather than simply stating that the manager should follow company policy.

questions.tips: Address both M and SM's positions, and explain how you'd manage each of them going forward.

questions.scenario:
We receive this email from the candidate:

"I sincerely apologize for missing the meeting scheduled at 6 PM today.

Just before the meeting, my laptop unexpectedly stopped working, and I also lost internet connectivity. By the time I was able to resolve both issues, it was around 7 PM. When I tried to access Slack afterward, I found that my account had been deactivated, so I was unable to contact you or the team there.

I'm really sorry for the inconvenience and for not being able to inform you beforehand. The situation was completely unexpected, and I wanted to explain what happened as soon as I could.

Please let me know if there is anything I need to do regarding my Slack access or the missed meeting."
questions.questionText: If you were their manager from the previous situation, what reply would you write? Explain your reasoning.
questions.placeholder: Write your reply and explain your reasoning...
questions.tips: Consider what you'd actually say to the candidate, not just how you'd feel about the situation.

questions.scenario:
At some point after sending that initial email, the candidate writes this:

"After the internet came back and my laptop started working again, I tried logging into Slack, but I couldn't understand why it wasn't letting me log in. I spent some time trying to figure out what was wrong, and eventually I realized that the account had been deactivated. That's when I understood that I needed to inform you about what had happened.

Around the same time, the laundry people came to the hostel, and I had to go there urgently. There was a very long queue, and it ended up taking half an hour.

After I came back, I had to work on some assignments as my exams are coming up and I had some pending work to finish. While I was working on my assignments, I suddenly realized that I had completely forgotten to send you an email explaining what had happened.

That's why there was such a long gap between the internet issue and the email. I understand that I should have informed you much earlier, but this is honestly how the delay happened."
questions.questionText: What reply would you write? Explain your reasoning.
questions.placeholder: Write your reply and explain your reasoning...
questions.tips: Consider how this new explanation should (or shouldn't) change your response.

questions.questionText:
We give new hires an end-of-week (EOW) team call, where they show what they've built. Here are some of our other existing team processes/rituals.

If you could make any additions to the EOW team call, what would you do?

The best answers will link the addition to our existing systems rather than inventing something disconnected from them.

supportingTabs.label: Existing Team Processes
supportingTabs.content:
Star Chart — an ongoing, visible way we track and recognise contributions.

Birthday Cakes — celebrated yearly, for each team member's birthday.

Team Meeting — held yearly.

End-of-Week (EOW) Team Call — where the team shows what they've built that week.

questions.placeholder: Describe your addition to the EOW team call and how it connects to our existing processes...
questions.tips: Link your idea to the existing systems (Star Chart, Birthday Cakes, Team Meeting) rather than proposing something disconnected from them.
